messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mark, a 34-year-old Navy Officer, traced his current difficulties back to a single night nine months ago. He had been stationed at a coastal base when the hurricane made landfall, far stronger than forecast. He and two dozen others took shelter in a concrete supply building, but the storm surge overwhelmed the flood barriers. He remembers the power failing, plunging them into a terrifying, echoing darkness. As the water rose rapidly in the confined space, the panicked crowd pressed in on him. For hours, he was pinned in a low crouch against a storage rack, the smell of rubbing alcohol from a makeshift first-aid kit sharp in the air as the water lapped at his chest.

In the weeks that followed, the event returned not as a coherent story, but in silent, disjointed pictures. He would see a flickering image of the churning, dark water, or the whites of someone's eyes in the brief sweep of a flashlight. These memories were so extreme that they felt fundamentally unreal, as if he were recalling a movie he had seen rather than something he had lived through. The most unsettling aspect was the physical reenactment; when an image would flash into his mind, his body would involuntarily tense, his back and legs locking into the same cramped, crouched position he had held for hours in the flooded building. This physical echo of the trauma reinforced his sense of profound alienation from his own body and past.

This sense of alienation began to bleed into all corners of his life. He had come to believe he was no longer the happy, capable person he had once been; that man, he felt, had been washed away in the flood. Each intrusive visual memory served as fresh evidence for this conclusion, a snapshot proving his permanent state of misery. The conviction that he was now irrevocably broken and isolated seemed to prime his mind for the memories, making them surface with greater frequency whenever he felt most alone. This deep-seated feeling of not belonging anywhere also made him hyper-aware of his surroundings, constantly scanning for things that felt unsafe, which only made him more likely to encounter the very cues he dreaded.

The world quickly became a landscape of hidden threats. A crowded mess hall on base would trigger a wave of panic, bringing with it a flash of the panicked bodies pressing in on him in the dark. The smell of alcohol on a colleague's breath after a social event would instantly make him feel a chasm open between them, reinforcing his belief that he was utterly set apart from others. In response to these triggers, he began to shrink his world. He started avoiding his friends, turning down invitations to go out. He made excuses to leave any circumstance that reminded him of the event, especially rooms that were dark or crowded. This avoidance was a desperate attempt to manage the overwhelm, but it came with a cost.

His strategies became a self-reinforcing prison. When a memory fragment surfaced, his immediate reaction was to withdraw from his wife and retreat into a punishing internal monologue, telling himself he deserved to suffer for his weakness. Yet, the very act of avoiding his friends would force him to confront why, which inevitably brought back the shared trauma and more intrusive images. His self-imposed isolation also made him more sensitive to his triggers; the more he thought about his fear of the dark, the more menacing the evening shadows in his own home became. The memories themselves also sharpened his sensitivity, so that after a particularly vivid flashback, the normal bustle of the base felt like a direct physical threat.

Mark finally sought help after his wife found him in his car in their driveway late one night, unable to bring himself to walk into the dark house where she was sleeping. His career, once a source of pride, was now precarious due to missed social obligations, and the emotional distance between him and his wife felt vast and unbridgeable. He described feeling like a ghost haunting his own life, a man who no longer belonged to his family, his friends, or the Navy. He confessed that what frightened him most was not the memory of the flood, but the terrifying certainty that the happy, confident man he used to be was gone for good, and he would be trapped in this miserable, isolated state forever.
